headline: Payrolls at 8:30. Waller's hold signal drove a 1% rally and broke the hike trade, but he pinned his September vote on August INFLATION, not jobs. Lululemon down 18%, Guidewire down 15%, Bitcoin holding a 5% jump.
client_frame_short:
The August jobs report comes out at 8:30 this morning, and the honest thing to say in advance is that nobody knows what it will say. The range of professional forecasts runs from a loss of 25,000 jobs to a gain of 125,000 - that is not a disagreement about a decimal point, it is a disagreement about whether the labour market is shrinking or growing. **When the spread of expert opinion is that wide, the number is not forecastable, and a portfolio built to survive only one of those outcomes is not a portfolio.** Last month's report showed a loss of 23,000 jobs, so a soft print would not be new information.

The more interesting development was yesterday. A Federal Reserve governor said he is inclined to hold rates steady this month, and markets took the odds of a September rate increase from about 61% down to about 51% - a coin flip. Stocks rose about 1%, the volatility index fell to 14, and Bitcoin jumped 5%. But read the fine print: he said his decision depends on next week's inflation data, not on this morning's jobs number. That is why we treat today as noise and next Friday's inflation report as the event that actually matters.
client_frame:
The August employment report arrives at 8:30 this morning, and the most useful thing to know about it is how little agreement there is about what it will show. Named professional forecasts run from a loss of 25,000 jobs (Fifth Third) to a gain of 125,000 at the top of the street range, with Wells Fargo at +80,000 and Goldman Sachs, Wolfe Research and Credit Agricole all clustered at +65,000. The Reuters poll of economists sits at +56,000. Last month's report showed payrolls FALLING by 23,000, and May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000. A spread that wide is itself the message: this is not a case where the market has a confident view that a surprise will disturb. Nobody knows, the range of honest professional opinion spans growth and contraction, and portfolios should be built to be indifferent to which number prints.

Yesterday's session is the more instructive story, and it turned on one speech. Federal Reserve Governor Christopher Waller said that recent data show 'some signs of disinflation' and that if that continues 'I would be inclined to support holding the target for the federal funds rate at its current setting' (Federal Reserve, speech text, September 3). Markets moved immediately: the odds of a September rate increase fell from about 61% to about 51% (CME FedWatch), the S&P 500 rose 1.06%, the Dow rose 1.18%, the volatility index fell nearly 6% to 14.32, and Bitcoin rose 5.1%. But the crucial sentence is the conditional one. Waller said his decision 'will be heavily influenced by what we learn about August inflation' and added that he does not expect the employment data 'to deviate much from what we have been seeing.' In other words, the Fed governor who moved the market yesterday told you in advance that this morning's jobs number is not what he is waiting for. Next Friday's inflation report is.

Underneath the rally, yesterday's data was mixed rather than good, and it is worth being precise about that. The ISM services survey came in at 55.4, comfortably expansionary - but its employment component contracted for a second straight month at 47.8, and its prices component printed 72.6, above 70 for the fifth time in six months (Institute for Supply Management). The trade deficit widened by $17.4bn in a single month to $88.6bn, a materially negative input for third-quarter growth (Census Bureau and Bureau of Economic Analysis). Jobless claims at 206,000 were a non-event. So the picture is contracting service-sector employment alongside firmly rising prices, which is an uncomfortable combination, and the equity market chose to trade the activity headline. Separately, the corporate news was harsh where it was harsh: Lululemon fell roughly 18% overnight after cutting its full-year outlook, and Guidewire fell about 15% on guidance for the second consecutive quarter.

For clients: today is a good example of a day that feels important and mostly is not. A single monthly employment estimate, with a forecast range spanning job losses to solid gains, will be revised twice and was pre-discounted by the Fed official who moved the market yesterday. The genuinely consequential events are next week - the producer price report on Thursday, the consumer price report on Friday, and the Federal Reserve meeting on the 15th and 16th, where the market currently prices a coin flip between a hold and one more increase. It is also worth restating the structural fact that gets lost in all of this: the market prices exactly zero probability of a rate CUT at any meeting between now and March 2027. Anyone still framing this year around when cuts arrive is anchored to a story the market abandoned months ago.

asia_close.name: Nikkei 225
asia_close.note: Closed up 806.46 points at 65,020.94, led by technology and electronics, and this was the first advance in five trading sessions. That detail matters for interpretation: Japan is bouncing off a losing streak into a Bank of Japan meeting the market expects to deliver a hike, which is a different setup from Korea or Hong Kong simply following the US tech tape. The 10-year JGB yield fell to 2.899% from 2.948%, easing the domestic discount-rate pressure that caused the losing streak in the first place.

asia_close.name: Hang Seng
asia_close.note: Up 436.80 points, attributed to the global technology rally and to reduced expectations of a September Federal Reserve increase. Aggregator sources disagree at the margin - one gives 25,650.87 and another 25,658.73 - so the level is precise to roughly ten points, not to the decimal, and the discrepancy is flagged rather than averaged away.

asia_close.name: KOSPI
asia_close.note: Up 107.73 points, with the KOSDAQ up 2.95% to 813.50. Korea is the most semiconductor-levered index in the region, so a 1.6% gain on the session after Broadcom's margin guide knocked the Philadelphia semiconductor index down 2.5% intraday is a meaningful vote that the AI capital-expenditure cycle is intact even where its profitability is being repriced. A second aggregator gives 6,690.72; the discrepancy is flagged.

asia_close.name: JGB 10Y
asia_close.note: The Japanese 10-year yield fell to 2.899% from 2.948%, with the session range 2.899% to 2.948% - the low is the close, so it fell steadily rather than spiking. Falling JGB yields alongside a yen that is still near a one-month high is the curve-flattening signature of a nearer-term Bank of Japan hike expectation: a September move supports the currency while pulling long-end term premium lower. No new Bank of Japan communication occurred inside the overnight window.

asia_close.name: Shanghai Composite
asia_close.note: The only materially lower board in Asia, down about half a percent, with the S&P/ASX 200 also down 0.2% at 9,005.90. China's decline against strong gains in Japan, Korea and Hong Kong confirms the overnight move was a technology and rate-expectations trade rather than a regional growth impulse. A second aggregator gives 3,930.12 for the Shanghai close; flagged.

europe_open.name: STOXX Europe 600
europe_open.note: Down 0.1% at 648.67 as of 07:10 GMT and down 0.2% at 648.08 by 08:38 GMT, against Thursday's 649.10 close. Europe is fading the US rally rather than joining it, which is the ordinary pre-payrolls posture. The sector split is the interesting part: autos rose 1.1% while chemicals and banks each fell almost 1%, a defensive rotation inside a flat index.

europe_open.name: DAX
europe_open.note: Marginally higher, against Thursday's close near 26,003. A precise Friday morning LEVEL is not published here: aggregator quotes for the DAX, FTSE 100 and Euro STOXX 50 conflicted materially at 07:00 ET - one page served a FTSE reading of +0.86% against Reuters' -0.1% at the same hour, and one Euro STOXX 50 quote was explicitly stamped as Thursday's close. Percentage moves with timestamps are reliable; single levels are not, so only the moves are given.

europe_open.name: FTSE 100
europe_open.note: Down 0.1% at 07:10 GMT against Thursday's close near 10,832, which is a mild underperformance rather than the outperformance it managed earlier in the week. The UK index is the most commodity-weighted large European board, so crude easing 0.5% to 0.8% overnight is a headwind here in a way it is not for the DAX.

europe_open.name: Volkswagen
europe_open.note: The single largest move in Europe. Volkswagen's supervisory board unanimously approved a transformation plan on Thursday that includes roughly 50,000 further job cuts and approximately halving the model range. The shares rose 6% and carried the European autos index up 1.1% in an otherwise flat tape. The market is paying for cost removal, which is a notable read on how European industrial equity is currently valued.

single_name_moves.note: Lululemon is the night's largest dislocation, down roughly 18% to about $100 from a $121.77 close. From the company's own release: net revenue FELL 4% to $2.416bn, comparable sales fell 9% with the Americas down 12%, and diluted EPS of $2.92 INCLUDED $0.86 per share of tariff refunds and associated interest - so the underlying quarter is closer to $2.06. Full-year guidance was cut to revenue of $10.35bn to $10.50bn, a 5% to 7% decline, with EPS of $9.48 to $9.73 against roughly $10.84 expected, and it assumes no further tariff refunds. This is a genuine consumer datapoint, not a margin-mix story: the top line is shrinking.

Guidewire fell roughly 15% to about $172.80 from a $202.86 close, and the range across vendor snapshots is a timing artifact rather than a disagreement - published as a range for that reason. From the company's release: Q4 revenue $411.1mn, up 15%, with subscription and support up 32%, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.99 against $0.81 a year ago, so the quarter beat. The problem is the guide - fiscal Q1 revenue of $372mn to $378mn against roughly $378mn expected. This is the SECOND consecutive quarter Guidewire has been punished on guidance, having fallen about 14% on its June print, which is the relevant pattern for anyone sizing post-earnings drift.

Samsara is the night's best large-cap move, up 15.6% to $44.79 pre-market and the only company above $2bn of market capitalisation in the pre-market top-20 gainers. From the company's release: revenue $508.4mn, up 30%, ending annual recurring revenue $2.125bn, up 30%, non-GAAP EPS of $0.20 against $0.12 a year ago and roughly $0.16 expected, a fourth consecutive quarter of GAAP profitability, and full-year revenue guidance of $2.043bn to $2.047bn. A clean beat-and-raise, and the move has held through the overnight session rather than fading.

Zscaler is deliberately published as a PATH rather than a price, because vendor snapshots of the after-hours tape disagree by more than ten percentage points - one shows +7.2% with a high near $201, another shows +1.3%, and a third describes modest profit-taking after an initial rise. The defensible statement is that it spiked hard immediately post-print and faded to roughly flat to up 1% later. The fundamentals are not in dispute: revenue $898.2mn, up 25%, annual recurring revenue $3.771bn, up 25%, non-GAAP EPS $1.19 against roughly $1.09 expected. The fade is explained by fiscal 2027 guidance of 17% ARR growth against 25% just delivered.

geo_headlines: Governor Christopher Waller's 8:30 speech on Thursday was the single event that turned the week, and it is worth reading what he actually said rather than the headline. His words: 'while inflation remains meaningfully above the Federal Open Market Committee's 2 percent goal, recent data suggest we are finally seeing some signs of disinflation,' and 'if this continues in the data due over the next two weeks, I would be inclined to support holding the target for the federal funds rate at its current setting.' He also gave the other side: 'if the incoming data for August show this improvement has been fleeting, then it may be appropriate to raise the policy rate when the FOMC meets on September 15 and 16.' The load-bearing sentence for today is the conditional: 'my decision on the appropriate stance of policy will be heavily influenced by what we learn about August inflation,' and separately, 'I don't expect that the employment data will deviate much from what we have been seeing.' Waller pre-committed to discounting this morning's payrolls print. That asymmetry is the most tradable fact on this page: a hot number can push hike odds up through other members of the Committee, but it cannot easily undo Waller's stated conditional hold.

The CME FedWatch distribution advanced to a September 3 reporting cohort and repriced dovish for a second consecutive session. The September 16 meeting now shows a 48.6% probability of a hold against a 51.4% probability of a 25 basis point HIKE - a coin flip, and a further ten-point dovish move from the 38.8/61.2 split on the prior cohort. Two sessions ago this board read 31/69. October 28 shows 35.7% hold, 50.7% for one hike and 13.7% for two. December 9 shows 15.9% hold, 42.4% one hike, 34.1% two hikes and 7.6% three. January 27 shows 12.6% hold. The single most important structural fact on this board has not changed and deserves restating to any client who still frames the year around easing: the probability of a rate CUT is exactly ZERO at every meeting through March 2027, because the distribution contains no bucket below the current 3.50 to 3.75 percent target band. The market's central case is at most one more hike followed by an extended pause. This week's argument has been about the timing and count of hikes, never their direction.

The August employment report lands at 8:30 this morning and the forecast dispersion is the story. Named, attributed estimates: Fifth Third at MINUS 25,000, the Reuters poll of economists at plus 56,000, a FactSet median of plus 65,000 from six contributors clustered between 50,000 and 70,000, Goldman Sachs at plus 65,000 headline with plus 40,000 private and 4.1% unemployment, Wolfe Research at plus 65,000, Credit Agricole at plus 65,000, Wells Fargo at plus 80,000, and a street range topping out near plus 125,000. That is a spread of 150,000 jobs. The prior month was a DECLINE of 23,000 with unemployment at 4.1%, participation at 61.4% and average hourly earnings up 3.2% year-on-year, and May and June were revised down by a combined 103,000. One clarification on a circulating figure: a 'Goldman plus 60,000 with 4.3% unemployment' number is a conflation - 4.3% is Goldman's year-end forecast, not its August call. This release does NOT contain the annual benchmark revision; that preliminary estimate came separately on August 28 at minus 79,000 nonfarm, and the final lands in February 2027.

Thursday's data was mixed to hawkish, not good, and the gap between the data and the 1% rally is the honest thing to flag. ISM services came in at 55.4 against 54.1 in July, with business activity at 61.7 and new orders at 60.9 - genuinely strong. But the employment sub-index contracted for a SECOND straight month at 47.8, and the prices index printed 72.6, its fifth reading above 70 in six months. Contracting service-sector employment alongside accelerating input prices is a stagflationary mix, and the equity market chose to trade the activity headline. The July trade deficit widened by $17.4bn in one month to $88.6bn as exports fell $6.6bn and imports rose $10.8bn - a materially negative third-quarter growth input that the tape ignored, though year-to-date the deficit is still down 29.6% on 2025. Jobless claims at 206,000 for the week ending August 29 were a non-event, up 2,000 with the prior week revised up 1,000. Second-quarter unit labour costs were revised DOWN to plus 1.2% from plus 1.3%, and manufacturing unit labour costs fell 0.3%, the first decline since 2021 - quietly the most supportive item for the disinflation case Waller was making.

Bitcoin rose 5.12% on Thursday to close at $81,263.99 and has given back nothing overnight, trading $81,128.99 at 07:12. The catalyst is the same Waller repricing that moved everything else, amplified by forced covering: more than $415mn of short positions were liquidated as the price took out $81,000, though venue tallies of the magnitude disagree substantially, so treat the existence of a squeeze as well supported and the size as unsettled. The timing is unambiguous - Bitcoin was near $77,900 at 8:00 in the morning and essentially the entire move happened after Waller crossed the wires. The equity read-through was the day's leadership: Robinhood was the largest gainer in the S&P 500, up nearly 16%, and Coinbase rose about 10%, though Robinhood had a separate non-crypto driver in a broker note on prediction markets. One circulating explanation for the move - that US and Iranian hostilities had paused - is contradicted by the primary record for the same morning, in which Iran struck US bases in Kuwait and the UAE, and it is not used here.

Thursday night's earnings cohort produced the two largest single-name dislocations of the week, and both were guidance, not results. Lululemon fell roughly 18% to about $100: revenue FELL 4% to $2.416bn, comparable sales fell 9% with the Americas down 12%, and its reported $2.92 of EPS included $0.86 of tariff refunds, so the underlying quarter is nearer $2.06. Full-year guidance was cut to a 5% to 7% revenue decline with EPS of $9.48 to $9.73 against roughly $10.84 expected. Guidewire fell about 15% despite beating, on a fiscal Q1 revenue guide of $372mn to $378mn against $378mn expected - its second consecutive guidance-driven drawdown after a similar 14% fall in June. On the other side, Samsara rose 15.6% on a clean beat-and-raise, UiPath rose 13%, DocuSign beat and raised and rose about 4% after peaking near 7%, and Smith and Wesson rose 11%. Asana fell 12% and Oxford Industries 15%. The dividing line across the whole cohort is not whether results beat but what the forward guide implies, which is the signature of a market with high embedded expectations and low tolerance for deceleration.

The semiconductor divergence on Thursday was single-name and mechanical rather than a break in the AI trade, and the shape of the session proves it. The Philadelphia semiconductor index closed up just 0.114% at 11,352.13 while the Nasdaq 100 rose 1.163% - but it traded as low as 11,056.38, roughly 2.5% down, and closed near its high of 11,371.33. So the underperformance was a morning shock almost entirely repaired. The cause was Broadcom, the heaviest weight in the index, which fell 2.74% to $357.16 after guiding fourth quarter gross margin to roughly 73% against 78% a year earlier, despite reporting revenue of $29.591bn and AI semiconductor revenue up 221% to $16.7bn. The rest of the complex was fine: NVIDIA rose 1.8% and announced the acquisition of Hugging Face for $12.93bn the same day, its second-largest purchase ever, confirming reporting that had circulated since late August. Broadcom traded back up about 1.2% overnight. Precise Thursday closes for other semiconductor names are NOT published here - the one page carrying them was describing Wednesday's session.

The Middle East was active inside the window but nothing that happened was new in kind, and the crude market's response is the evidence. Iran conducted a missile and drone attack on US bases in Kuwait and the UAE early Thursday - Ahmad al Jaber Air Base and al Minhad Air Base - and a US defence official said no US bases were impacted; Kuwaiti air defences intercepted, and Kuwait's defence ministry called it blatant Iranian aggression. That followed Iranian strikes on US bases in Kuwait, Jordan, Bahrain and Iraq on September 2. Israel's defence minister said Israel would target Iranian infrastructure including ENERGY infrastructure if Iran attacked Israel, while senior Israeli officials said they had not observed near-term Iranian intent to strike Israel. Overnight the US disabled three vessels and redirected 87 in the ongoing blockade. Yet Brent is DOWN 0.53% at $95.01 and WTI down 0.83% at $90.54, both still on track for their strongest weekly gain since mid-July. The escalation was priced earlier in the week; the overnight tape is fading it. Katz's energy-infrastructure threat remains the unpriced tail.

Two absences are worth recording explicitly, because an absence is a finding. First, TARIFFS: no new tariff development occurred inside the overnight window. The live backdrop is entirely pre-existing - Canada's counter-tariff package of roughly C$27.6bn takes effect at 12:01 on September 8 at rates of 15, 25 and 50 percent, and the India and Russian-oil friction continues. The one tariff item that actually moved a stock was corporate rather than policy: $0.86 of Lululemon's quarterly EPS was tariff refunds, and its full-year guide assumes no further ones. Second, the BANK OF JAPAN: no new policy communication occurred inside the window. Governor Ueda's comment that the Bank will debate a hike at every meeting including September 17 and 18 came on September 1 and 2, BEFORE this window opened. So the overnight yen move is positioning, not fresh policy news. What is new is that Japan's top currency diplomat Atsushi Mimura said Friday he remains alert to exchange-rate moves and is in constant contact with US authorities, which keeps two-way intervention risk live at these levels.

Next week is where the consequential events actually sit, and the calendar needs three corrections to what has been circulating. The Bank of Canada does NOT announce on September 9 - the Bank's published 2026 fixed dates put September on the 2nd, where it already held at 2.25 percent, and September 16 carries only the Summary of Deliberations. The European Central Bank decision is Thursday September 10 at 8:15 with the press conference at 8:45, in Berlin, and it is a HIKE rather than a cut: all 65 economists in the Reuters poll expect 25 basis points to 2.50 percent. Consumer credit is not today but Tuesday September 8 at 3:00, because Labor Day pushes the fifth business day out. The two prints that matter are the producer price report on Thursday and the consumer price report on Friday September 11 - the last major inflation reading before the FOMC on the 15th and 16th, and the exact data Waller said his vote depends on. Oracle and Adobe both report after the close on September 10. The Federal Reserve communications blackout begins tomorrow, Saturday September 5, so Waller was the last policy voice the market hears.
